newsitem.title: USA: Conrail/CSX deal seen surviving court challenge.
newsitem.headline: Conrail/CSX deal seen surviving court challenge.

text.p: Conrail Inc's board is pushing the legal limits in agreeing to stay away from all suitors other than CSX Corp for two years, but the move may well survive a court challenge, legal experts said.

Norfolk Southern Corp, seeking to snatch Conrail from CSX with a rival bid, has challenged the "exclusivity" provision in the Conrail-CSX merger agreement which obligates the two railroads to refrain from discussing a third-party offer "to...December 31, 1998."
The exclusivity period was extended from July 1997 as part of an increased bid by CSX announced Thursday, and drew an immediate court challenge from Norfolk Southern.

Papers incorporating the challenge into an existing suit seeking to block the CSX-Conrail merger were to be filed Friday with the U.S. District Court for Eastern Pennsylvania, Norfolk Southern attorneys said.

Some analysts and investors said if the provision were not thrown out after a January 9 court hearing before U.S. District Judge Donald Van Artsdalen, it could guarantee a victory for CSX in the takeover battle because shareholders could not wait for two years for a deal with Norfolk Southern.

The case will hinge on whether Conrail's agreeing to the extended exclusivity period remains within the broad discretion allowed a corporate board under Pennsylvania law, said Charles Yablon, a professor of corporate law at Cardozo University in New York, said.
"They're pushing the outside of the envelope, and trying to take maximum advantage of the leeway that Pennsylvania law gives them," Yablon said.

"(If) CSX and Conrail can put forward a plausible reason why they need this provision...and show that it's in the best interest of any of the corporate constituencies, it will probably be all right," he said.
He said the expiration date appeared to be extended in part to allow time for the regulatory process of considering the merger to be completed.
Last month, Van Artsdalen upheld the provision setting the exclusivity period to July, as part of a ruling denying Norfolk Southern's request for an emergency injunction blocking the merger.

Conrail had said then its agreement not to talk with another buyer was necessary to draw a good price from CSX and prevent it from making a joint bid for Conrail with Norfolk Southern. "Directors have every right to favor one competing bid over another," Van Artsdalen said. "And certainly it seems to me that it (Conrail) can agree not to shop their (CSX's) proposal after signing a merger agreement."
However, Norfolk Southern attorney Steven Rothschild called the newly extended period "outrageous." He said its length, unprecedented in his experience, made it unjustifiable.
"I just think there comes a time where the court is likely to say enough is enough," Rothschild said.
Conrail said Norfolk Southern's legal action was "entirely without merit."

Said Eric Orts, a University of Pennsylvania Wharton School professor and expert on Pennsylvania corporate law who has been hired as a consultant by Conrail, "I think Pennsylvania gives greater protection to a friendly deal like this...I'm fairly confident that they (Conrail) are going to be able to win in this current court case."
Said a source involved in the CSX-Conrail transaction, "CSX is totally confident in its legal opinion. There is no question in the minds of the legal advisors of both companies."
Rothschild said that at the January 9 hearing, Norfolk Southern also will argue that Conrail and CSX have triggered a provision in Pennsylvania law that would require CSX to pay all cash for Conrail.

In addition, he had said earlier this week that Norfolk Southern could also take its battle for Conrail to other forums, such as the federal Surface Transportation Board, which must approve the Conrail-CSX merger.
